items.stem: Explain why clay particles need a higher velocity to be entrained than sand particles.
items.answer: Clay particles are cohesive (stick together by electrostatic forces) and lie within the smooth laminar layer near the bed, so a high velocity is needed to lift them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cohesion; 1 mark bed roughness/laminar layer [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between competence and capacity.
items.answer: Competence is the largest particle size that can be moved at a given velocity; capacity is the total quantity of load that can be carried at a given discharge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 gives values read from the Hjulström curve for four particle sizes: Fine silt (0.01 mm): critical erosion velocity 60 cm/s, settling velocity 0.008 cm/s. Coarse sand (1 mm): critical erosion velocity 30 cm/s, settling velocity 9 cm/s. Granules (3 mm): critical erosion velocity 60 cm/s, settling velocity 20 cm/s. Pebbles (20 mm): critical erosion velocity 150 cm/s, settling velocity 90 cm/s. The mean velocity of a river is 100 cm/s. Explain why the critical erosion velocity for clay is higher than for sand.
items.answer: Clay is cohesive and its particles lie in the laminar layer close to a smooth bed, so more energy is needed to lift them.

items.stem: Table 3.1 gives values read from the Hjulström curve for four particle sizes: Fine sand (0.1 mm): critical erosion velocity 25 cm/s, settling velocity 0.8 cm/s. Granules (3 mm): critical erosion velocity 60 cm/s, settling velocity 20 cm/s. Pebbles (20 mm): critical erosion velocity 150 cm/s, settling velocity 90 cm/s. Cobbles (100 mm): critical erosion velocity 330 cm/s, settling velocity 200 cm/s. The mean velocity of a river is 0.5 cm/s. (a) Explain why the critical erosion velocity for clay is higher than for sand. (b) Suggest how the river’s load would change if velocity fell to 1 cm/s.
items.answer: (a) Clay is cohesive and its particles lie in the laminar layer close to a smooth bed, so more energy is needed to lift them. (b) Most sand and all coarser particles would be deposited; only silt and clay would stay in suspension (plus the dissolved load).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark deposition of coarse; 1 mark fines remain [2]

items.stem: Daniel argues that velocity is the most important factor influencing erosion, transport and deposition in a river channel. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to the Hjulström curve, load and discharge.
items.answer: For: Hjulström curve: entrainment, transport and settling depend on velocity; floods do most work; deposition when velocity falls on meander insides and at river mouths. Against: Discharge and channel shape (hydraulic radius) control efficiency; load supply, particle size and cohesion, bedrock type, gradient and human activity (dams trapping sediment) also matter. Conclusion: Velocity is the immediate control, but it is itself controlled by discharge, gradient and channel efficiency, and load supply limits what is actually moved.

items.stem: Explain why rivers often flow faster in their lower course than in upland streams.
items.answer: Upland channels are rough, shallow and boulder-strewn with a low hydraulic radius, so much energy is lost to friction; lower channels are deeper, smoother and more efficient with greater discharge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark roughness; 1 mark hydraulic radius; 1 mark discharge [3]

items.stem: Explain the formation of a knickpoint on a long profile.
items.answer: A fall in base level (sea-level fall or uplift) rejuvenates the river, which cuts down from the mouth; a break of slope marks the junction between the old and new profiles and migrates upstream; also hard rock bands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause; 1 mark downcutting; 1 mark migration [3]

items.stem: Tomás argues that channel efficiency is more important than gradient in explaining river velocity. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Hydraulic radius and roughness control friction losses; lowland rivers such as the Amazon flow quickly on very low gradients. Against: Gradient provides the potential energy; steep mountain torrents can flow fast in floods; discharge, load and bedrock also influence velocity. Conclusion: Over the length of most rivers efficiency and discharge outweigh the fall in gradient, so velocity tends to rise downstream, but locally gradient can dominate.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a meander.
items.answer: Riffle-pool sequences develop; flow is deflected to alternate banks; helicoidal flow erodes the outer bank (river cliff) by hydraulic action and abrasion where velocity is highest, and carries sediment to the inner bank to form a point bar; the bend migrates and becomes more pronounced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each stage up to [4]

items.stem: Explain how a floodplain is formed.
items.answer: Lateral erosion by migrating meanders widens the valley floor; deposition of point bars; overbank deposition of silt during floods builds up layers of alluvium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark lateral erosion; 1 mark point bars; 1 mark flood deposits [3]

items.stem: Explain why channelisation in one place may increase flood risk elsewhere.
items.answer: Faster flow carries the flood peak downstream more quickly and concentrates it, increasing peaks in unprotected settlements downstream.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “meander”?
options: A sinuous bend in a river channel, with a river cliff on the outer bank and a point bar on the inner bank.
A shallow section of a channel with coarse deposits and fast, turbulent flow.
The corkscrew-like flow in a meander that moves water across the channel from the outer to the inner bank along the bed.
A deposit of sand and gravel on the inside of a meander bend, where velocity is low.
items.answer: A sinuous bend in a river channel, with a river cliff on the outer bank and a point bar on the inner bank.

items.stem: Explain the conditions needed for a delta to form.
items.answer: Large sediment load; velocity drops on entering standing water; low tidal range and weak currents; flocculation of clay in salt water; shallow offshore gradient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per condition [3]

items.stem: Name a case study of a river landform or delta you have studied. For your example, describe the opportunities and challenges the landform presents for people.
items.answer: the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, Bangladesh: Home to over 150 million people; fertile alluvium for rice; frequent floods and cyclones (e.g. Cyclone Sidr 2007); sea-level rise, subsidence and dams upstream (Farakka barrage) reduce sediment supply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Farming, settlement, hazards, human impacts, with figures. [5]

items.stem: Fig. 3.3 is a map of a river. Measurements for several reaches are: Reach A: channel length 5.4 km, straight-line distance 4.7 km. Reach B: channel length 1.7 km, straight-line distance 1.6 km. Reach C: channel length 1.9 km, straight-line distance 1.9 km. (a) Calculate the sinuosity index of each reach. (b) Suggest why straightening a meandering reach could increase flood risk downstream.
items.answer: (a) Reach A 1.15; Reach B 1.06; Reach C 1 (b) A shorter, steeper and smoother channel carries water downstream faster, so flood peaks arrive sooner and higher downstream.
items.markingKey: (a) channel length ÷ straight-line distance; 1 mark half correct, 2 marks all [2] (b) 1 mark faster flow; 1 mark downstream peak [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that deposition is more important than erosion in the formation of river landforms? In your answer you may refer to levees, floodplains and deltas.
items.answer: For: Point bars, levees, floodplains, deltas and braided bars are depositional; floodplain alluvium is built by repeated floods. Against: Meanders, river cliffs, oxbow lakes and floodplains also need lateral erosion; waterfalls, gorges and potholes are erosional; most landforms involve both. Conclusion: Most lowland landforms are the result of erosion and deposition acting together, though depositional processes dominate in the lower course and in deltas.

items.stem: A student writes: “A 100-year flood can only happen once a century.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It has a 1% chance in any year, so two can occur in consecutive years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why river restoration is increasingly used in HICs.
items.answer: Restores habitats and biodiversity, slows flow and stores water on floodplains, is cheaper to maintain than hard engineering, improves amenity; e.g. the River Skerne (UK) or the Isar in Munich.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason [3]

items.stem: Table 3.4 lists the six largest annual peak discharges (m³/s) in a 29-year record for the River Kelani (Sri Lanka): 2012: 1069, 2006: 1035, 2019: 874, 1999: 748, 2004: 657, 2005: 562. Calculate the recurrence interval of the 657 m³/s flood.
items.answer: 6 years

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that soft engineering is a more sustainable way of managing river floods than hard engineering?
items.answer: For: Wetland restoration, afforestation, floodplain zoning and making space for water work with natural processes, are cheaper to maintain and improve habitats (e.g. Netherlands Room for the River). Against: Soft methods need large areas of land and cannot protect existing dense cities; hard engineering such as the Thames Barrier or the Three Gorges Dam protects millions and high-value property. Conclusion: A combined, catchment-wide approach is most sustainable: soft engineering upstream and on floodplains, with hard engineering where high-value urban areas need protection.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the wearing down of load particles as they collide with each other, becoming smaller and rounder”.
items.answer: Attrition
items.markingKey: Attrition: the wearing down of load particles as they collide with each other, becoming smaller and rounder. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Once particles are entrained, they can be carried at velocities lower than those needed to pick them up.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. The transport field on the Hjulström curve lies between the settling and erosion velocity curves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the difference between competence and capacity. (b) Explain why clay particles need a higher velocity to be entrained than sand particles.
items.answer: (a) Competence is the largest particle size that can be moved at a given velocity; capacity is the total quantity of load that can be carried at a given discharge. (b) Clay particles are cohesive (stick together by electrostatic forces) and lie within the smooth laminar layer near the bed, so a high velocity is needed to lift them.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark cohesion; 1 mark bed roughness/laminar layer [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 gives values read from the Hjulström curve for four particle sizes: Coarse sand (1 mm): critical erosion velocity 30 cm/s, settling velocity 9 cm/s. Granules (3 mm): critical erosion velocity 60 cm/s, settling velocity 20 cm/s. Pebbles (20 mm): critical erosion velocity 150 cm/s, settling velocity 90 cm/s. Cobbles (100 mm): critical erosion velocity 330 cm/s, settling velocity 200 cm/s. The mean velocity of a river is 250 cm/s. Suggest how the river’s load would change if velocity fell to 1 cm/s.
items.answer: Most sand and all coarser particles would be deposited; only silt and clay would stay in suspension (plus the dissolved load).
items.markingKey: 1 mark deposition of coarse; 1 mark fines remain [2]

items.stem: Students tested the hypothesis that the mean size of bed load decreases with distance downstream. They measured the long axis of 20 pebbles at each of 10 sites along a river in northern Spain. Table 2.2 gives, for each site, the distance downstream from the source (km) and the mean pebble long axis (mm). Site 1: 1.3, 132. Site 2: 4.5, 127. Site 3: 6.3, 107. Site 4: 14, 96. Site 5: 20, 84. Site 6: 20.5, 55. Site 7: 27.2, 58. Site 8: 29.5, 52. Site 9: 34.3, 22. Site 10: 37.7, 12. Critical values of rs for n = 10: 0.564 (0.05 level) and 0.745 (0.01 level). Suggest one limitation of the method and how the investigation could be improved.
items.answer: Sampling may be biased towards larger, easily picked pebbles; use random sampling (e.g. a quadrat grid) and more pebbles per site; tributaries may add coarse load.
items.markingKey: 1 mark limitation; 1 mark improvement [2]

items.stem: A student measured roundness of bed load (Cailleux roundness index) at 10 sites downstream on a river in the Lake District, UK. Table 2.1 gives, for each site, the distance downstream (km) and the mean roundness index. Site 1: 2.8, 150. Site 2: 4.7, 217. Site 3: 9.3, 283. Site 4: 14.6, 481. Site 5: 15.5, 433. Site 6: 16.3, 458. Site 7: 16.7, 453. Site 8: 20.7, 543. Site 9: 20.8, 564. Site 10: 23.3, 590. Critical values of rs for n = 10: 0.564 (0.05 level) and 0.745 (0.01 level). (a) State a suitable null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Suggest reasons for the relationship shown by the data.
items.answer: (a) There is no relationship between the distance downstream (km) and the mean roundness index. (b) Attrition and abrasion knock off edges as particles collide and are moved downstream, so particles become rounder with distance travelled.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark per developed reason [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “A river can have more than one channel at the same point.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe how channel shape changes downstream.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Braided channels divide around bars of sediment. (b) Width, depth and cross-sectional area increase; hydraulic radius increases; channels become smoother and more efficient; gradient decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A long profile of a river shows the following heights above sea level: 0 km from the source: 507 m, 5 km from the source: 326 m, 29 km from the source: 203 m, 54 km from the source: 130 m. Suggest two reasons why a real profile may not be smooth.
items.answer: Bands of resistant rock forming waterfalls or rapids; lakes; rejuvenation knickpoints; tributary deposition; dams.

items.stem: “Channel efficiency is more important than gradient in explaining river velocity.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to gradient and discharge.
items.answer: For: Hydraulic radius and roughness control friction losses; lowland rivers such as the Amazon flow quickly on very low gradients. Against: Gradient provides the potential energy; steep mountain torrents can flow fast in floods; discharge, load and bedrock also influence velocity. Conclusion: Over the length of most rivers efficiency and discharge outweigh the fall in gradient, so velocity tends to rise downstream, but locally gradient can dominate.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “point bar”?

The corkscrew-like flow in a meander that moves water across the channel from the outer to the inner bank along the bed.
A deep section of a channel, often on the outside of a meander bend.
A shallow section of a channel with coarse deposits and fast, turbulent flow.
items.answer: A deposit of sand and gravel on the inside of a meander bend, where velocity is low.

items.stem: Explain the formation of an oxbow lake.
items.answer: Erosion on outer banks narrows the meander neck; during a flood the river cuts through the neck, taking the shorter route; deposition seals the ends of the old loop, leaving a lake that may become a swamp (meander scar).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each stage [3]

items.answer: (a) Reach A 2.12; Reach B 1.22; Reach C 1.91 (b) Helicoidal flow and erosion of outer banks with deposition on inner banks (point bars); bends migrate and grow; low gradient and cohesive banks favour meandering.

items.stem: Using a named example of a river landform or delta you have studied, explain how the landform developed. To what extent is your chosen example typical of a river landform or delta?
items.answer: Model answer (the Nile delta, Egypt): A classic arcuate delta about 240 km wide, formed by sediment from the Ethiopian Highlands; built by the Rosetta and Damietta distributaries. Holds about 40% of Egypt’s population and most farmland; since the Aswan High Dam (1970) traps sediment, the coast retreats by up to 100 m a year in places such as Rosetta; salinisation and subsidence.

items.answer: Correct. People build behind levees; when they are overtopped, as in New Orleans in 2005, damage is greater.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Dams have no effect on rivers downstream.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They trap sediment, alter regimes and cause downstream channel erosion and delta retreat.

items.stem: Referring to the Yangtze River, China or another example of flood management, evaluate how successful the flood management has been. To what extent is your chosen example typical of flood management?
items.answer: Model answer (the Yangtze River, China): The Three Gorges Dam (2006-2012) with 22 billion m³ of flood storage; dykes along the middle reaches; flood diversion areas such as Jingjiang; returning farmland to lakes. Reduced peak flows in 2010 and 2020 floods but could not prevent damage from heavy rain on downstream tributaries in 2020; 1.3 million people relocated; sediment trapped and downstream erosion.
